seen-1.text:
Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.
seen-1.reference: NCTB English for Today, Class 6, revised 2026, Lesson 5, printed [14, 15], PDF [18, 20].

seen-2.text: My first day at the new school was interesting. I was going to school with my father in a rickshaw. We reached school after fifteen minutes. My father said goodbye and left me at the school gate. I went in and found that everyone had gone to class. I walked into my classroom and found a seat. After some time a teacher came and warmly greeted us. I found the students very friendly in my new class.

textbook-poems.text:
Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

tasks.instruction:
Complete a story on The Bag at the School Gate. Read the opening and complete the story in at least ten new sentences. Give a suitable title. (10)
One afternoon, Rafi was leaving school when he noticed a small bag near the gate. He looked around, but nobody seemed to be looking for it. He decided to ask an adult for help.
tasks.answer:
The Bag at the School Gate
Rafi stopped beside the bag. He did not know who owned it. He called the teacher who was standing near the gate. Together, they took the bag to the school office. The teacher checked for a name while Rafi waited. A label inside named a pupil from another class. The office contacted that pupil’s class teacher. Soon a worried child arrived and described the bag. The teachers checked that it was really hers before returning it. She thanked Rafi for reporting what he had found. Rafi felt pleased that he had asked for help instead of guessing.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.

tasks.instruction: Write a dialogue on An object whose label has incomplete information. Write a dialogue between a pupil and a museum guide about an object whose label has incomplete information. (10)
tasks.answer:
Pupil: Excuse me, may I ask about this basket?
Guide: Of course. What would you like to know?
Pupil: The label describes its use, but I cannot find a date. When was it made?
Guide: I do not have a confirmed date at the moment.
Pupil: Should I write an approximate year in my notebook?
Guide: Please write that the date is not given. We should not guess.
Pupil: Is there another source we could check?
Guide: I can check the museum records and ask the curator.
Pupil: Thank you. I will keep the question in my notes.
Guide: You are welcome. Asking careful questions is part of learning.

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.

textbook-poems.text:
Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. textbook-poems.text:
Stop, Look, and Listen
No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

tasks.instruction:
Complete a story on The Bag at the School Gate. Read the opening and complete the story in at least ten new sentences. Give a suitable title. (10)
One afternoon, Rafi was leaving school when he noticed a small bag near the gate. He looked around, but nobody seemed to be looking for it. He decided to ask an adult for help.
tasks.answer:
The Bag at the School Gate
Rafi stopped beside the bag. He did not know who owned it. He called the teacher who was standing near the gate. Together, they took the bag to the school office. The teacher checked for a name while Rafi waited. A label inside named a pupil from another class. The office contacted that pupil’s class teacher. Soon a worried child arrived and described the bag. The teachers checked that it was really hers before returning it. She thanked Rafi for reporting what he had found. Rafi felt pleased that he had asked for help instead of guessing.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.

tasks.answer:
Pupil: Excuse me, may I ask about this basket?
Guide: Of course. What would you like to know?
Pupil: The label describes its use, but I cannot find a date. When was it made?
Guide: I do not have a confirmed date at the moment.
Pupil: Should I write an approximate year in my notebook?
Guide: Please write that the date is not given. We should not guess.
Pupil: Is there another source we could check?
Guide: I can check the museum records and ask the curator.
Pupil: Thank you. I will keep the question in my notes.
Guide: You are welcome. Asking careful questions is part of learning.

seen-1.text:
Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.

textbook-poems.text:
Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.

seen-1.text:
Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.

textbook-poems.text:
Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Stop, Look, and Listen
No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?

On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

Some guests will visit Imran's house tonight. So Imran's mother will cook dinner for them. She asks Imran to go to the local market. He often forgets to buy the necessary items. So his mother is making a shopping list for him. He is helping his mother make the list. Imran: Maa, what do I need to buy? Maa: Well, see if we have enough potatoes? Imran: We have some potatoes but I don't think it's enough. Maa: Then get half kg. of potatoes. How about tomatoes? Imran: I don't see any tomatoes. Maa: Are there any other vegetables? Imran: Yes, there are some beans, carrots, cucumber and eggplants. ... That's all. Maa: Well, I'll need one kg. of tomatoes. Half kg. of beans and two cauliflowers.... Are there any eggs, dear? Imran: There are only three eggs. Maybe I'll buy a dozen more? Maa: Humm..... oh, yes.... get some sugar and milk and one litre of oil, too. Imran: OK. One litre of milk and.... one kg. of sugar. Maa: One more thing, dear. You are forgetting your list! Here it is. Imran: Oh! Thanks, Maa.

I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.

Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

Complete a story on The Bag at the School Gate. Read the opening and complete the story in at least ten new sentences. Give a suitable title. (10)
One afternoon, Rafi was leaving school when he noticed a small bag near the gate. He looked around, but nobody seemed to be looking for it. He decided to ask an adult for help.
tasks.answer:
The Bag at the School Gate
Rafi stopped beside the bag. He did not know who owned it. He called the teacher who was standing near the gate. Together, they took the bag to the school office. The teacher checked for a name while Rafi waited. A label inside named a pupil from another class. The office contacted that pupil’s class teacher. Soon a worried child arrived and described the bag. The teachers checked that it was really hers before returning it. She thanked Rafi for reporting what he had found. Rafi felt pleased that he had asked for help instead of guessing.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.

Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

textbook-poems.text:
Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Stop, Look, and Listen
No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

seen-2.text: Bangladesh is a small country but it is gifted with unlimited natural attractions. Only some of these eye-catching destinations are known to us. But there are many other areas lying in the green, remote countryside that are less-known to us. Shusong Durgapur of Birishiri is one such place. Shusong Durgapur has an amazing landscape. It is located on the bank of crystal clear Someshwari river and is close to the Garo Hills. You can see the hills of Indian state of Meghalaya from here. The nature has unfolded its glory in this small, rural landscape. Here you can see the ceramic mountain leaning against the sky, the blue water of the pictorial mountain-valley, the modest movement of the river Someshwari, and the abandoned coal mines. There is another river here called Kangsa which is also known as old Someshwari. Shusong Durgapur is located under Netrokona district about 170 km north from Dhaka. Along with its scenic beauty this place is home to diverse indigenous groups: Hajong, Garo, Achik and Mandi. The cultural academy in Durgapur is responsible for preserving and promoting the culture and traditions of these indigenous groups. The main attraction of Birishiri is the ceramic hill of Durgapur and the charming landscape along the Shomeshwari River. The river changes its colour as the seasons change. Among other attractions are the palace of the Susang king, the Dasha Busha Temple, Orange Gardens, Shal forests and the Ramkrisna and Loknath Baba Temples. The best way to get to Birishiri is by road from Dhaka. You can find direct bus to Birishiri from Mohakhali bus stand, Dhaka. It usually takes 5 to 6 hours to get there. When you are there, you can go around the town by rickshaws. The rickshaw-pullers know all the places very well.

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.

seen-2.text: Once, a lion was sitting beside a river. Suddenly he looked at his own reflection and thought "My mane is too old. I need a new hairstyle!" The lion then roared "I'm the king of the jungle and this unruly mane does not fit a king." He dipped his paw into the river and tried desperately to smooth his mane. "Flap it all up. That will suit you!" the zebra said. "Yes, it will even look better with a bit of colour to match your moustache," the giraffe added. "What about a few ribbons?" the vulture asked. Then cried the hyena, "I know, a paper crown is what you need!" A snake was passing by silently. Seeing the king there he simply raised his head. "What do you think I should do, snake?" The king asked. "If a king is a wise king, nobody cares about his hairstyle," the snake said with a hissing sound. The king stared at the snake for some time. Then he smiled and kissed the snake. "Oh, why am I so vain? Am I not the king of the jungle?" roared the lion. He shook his head from side to side to shake his mane back into place. "From now on, I promise to be a wise king and not bother about my looks!" the lion roared.

textbook-poems.text:
The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Stop, Look, and Listen
No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

seen-2.text: Mariam is a student of class six in a government school in Rajshahi. Her mother works in an office and her father is a businessman. Mariam is very fond of her aunt, her father's sister, Suraiya Begum who lives in another part of the same town. On Fridays, she often goes to her aunt's place and spends time with her. Suraiya Begum is a retired school teacher. She is a widow and lives alone. Her husband died three years ago. Her two daughters are married and live with their families abroad. They talk to her over telephone and come to visit her whenever they get time. Suraiya Begum has a lot of free time. She spends her time in reading books, watching TV, visiting friends and relatives. Sometimes she writes letters to her old colleagues. But now a days she often gets bored of doing all these things. She wants to do something more meaningful, something that would do good to others. She is planning to establish an old people's home in her locality. She knows some elderly people live all alone. They have no one to take care of them. They often feel helpless and miserable. They need care and support. As part of her plan, Suraiya Begum starts to visit families. She talks to a number of people. She tries to find out the problems of elderly people in their families. She understands that old people are lonely and often they become sick. They have nobody to look after them. On Fridays, she often takes Mariam with her on these visits. Mariam has already become very friendly with some of the old men and women. They all love her very much. She tells them about her school and friends, her studies, her family. And they often tell her funny stories, fairy tales and ghost stories.

passages.text:
Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.

Mariam is a student of class six in a government school in Rajshahi. Her mother works in an office and her father is a businessman. Mariam is very fond of her aunt, her father's sister, Suraiya Begum who lives in another part of the same town. On Fridays, she often goes to her aunt's place and spends time with her. Suraiya Begum is a retired school teacher. She is a widow and lives alone. Her husband died three years ago. Her two daughters are married and live with their families abroad. They talk to her over telephone and come to visit her whenever they get time. Suraiya Begum has a lot of free time. She spends her time in reading books, watching TV, visiting friends and relatives. Sometimes she writes letters to her old colleagues. But now a days she often gets bored of doing all these things. She wants to do something more meaningful, something that would do good to others. She is planning to establish an old people's home in her locality. She knows some elderly people live all alone. They have no one to take care of them. They often feel helpless and miserable. They need care and support. As part of her plan, Suraiya Begum starts to visit families. She talks to a number of people. She tries to find out the problems of elderly people in their families. She understands that old people are lonely and often they become sick. They have nobody to look after them. On Fridays, she often takes Mariam with her on these visits. Mariam has already become very friendly with some of the old men and women. They all love her very much. She tells them about her school and friends, her studies, her family. And they often tell her funny stories, fairy tales and ghost stories.

Stop, Look, and Listen
No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

textbook-poems.text:
Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

subitems.text: [Let's Play] What mood does the poem create? Give a supporting detail.
subitems.answer: It creates a joyful, playful mood. The children welcome the end of school and invite one another to run and laugh.

tasks.instruction:
Complete a story on The Bag at the School Gate. Read the opening and complete the story in at least ten new sentences. Give a suitable title. (10)
One afternoon, Rafi was leaving school when he noticed a small bag near the gate. He looked around, but nobody seemed to be looking for it. He decided to ask an adult for help.
tasks.answer:
The Bag at the School Gate
Rafi stopped beside the bag. He did not know who owned it. He called the teacher who was standing near the gate. Together, they took the bag to the school office. The teacher checked for a name while Rafi waited. A label inside named a pupil from another class. The office contacted that pupil’s class teacher. Soon a worried child arrived and described the bag. The teachers checked that it was really hers before returning it. She thanked Rafi for reporting what he had found. Rafi felt pleased that he had asked for help instead of guessing.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.

tasks.instruction: Write a dialogue on An object whose label has incomplete information. Write a dialogue between a pupil and a museum guide about an object whose label has incomplete information. (10)
tasks.answer:
Pupil: Excuse me, may I ask about this basket?
Guide: Of course. What would you like to know?
Pupil: The label describes its use, but I cannot find a date. When was it made?
Guide: I do not have a confirmed date at the moment.
Pupil: Should I write an approximate year in my notebook?
Guide: Please write that the date is not given. We should not guess.
Pupil: Is there another source we could check?
Guide: I can check the museum records and ask the curator.
Pupil: Thank you. I will keep the question in my notes.
Guide: You are welcome. Asking careful questions is part of learning.

seen-2.text: Hason Raja was born in 1854, into a wealthy landlord family in Sylhet. He did not receive much formal education as a child. In his youth, he lived a life of luxury. He had everything - money, comfort and pleasure. However, at one point in his life, he began to feel that these material possessions were meaningless. He gave away all his property and started to think deeply about the creator, life, death and humankind. He wrote about a thousand songs which reflected his thoughts. In 1906, he published a book called Hason Udash. The book had 206 songs in it. In his songs, he called himself 'Crazy Hason Raja', or 'Pagla Hason Raja'. Another volume called Hason Raja Samagra (Complete Works of Hason Raja) was also published, which contained 500 poems and songs. Hason Raja's songs had always been popular in Sylhet, but very soon they spread all over Bangladesh and beyond. As you grow older, try to learn more about this great mystic poet through reading and listening to his songs.

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

textbook-poems.text:
Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Stop, Look, and Listen
No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.

One afternoon, Rafi was leaving school when he noticed a small bag near the gate. He looked around, but nobody seemed to be looking for it. He decided to ask an adult for help.
tasks.answer:
The Bag at the School Gate
Rafi stopped beside the bag. He did not know who owned it. He called the teacher who was standing near the gate. Together, they took the bag to the school office. The teacher checked for a name while Rafi waited. A label inside named a pupil from another class. The office contacted that pupil’s class teacher. Soon a worried child arrived and described the bag. The teachers checked that it was really hers before returning it. She thanked Rafi for reporting what he had found. Rafi felt pleased that he had asked for help instead of guessing.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
tasks.answer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.

seen-1.text:
Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.

seen-2.text: Today, I'd like to tell you about an interesting young man I met here. His name is Ashar Santoso. He was born in Indonesia. When he was eight, he moved to Singapore with his parents and went to a Singaporean school. After a few years, he went to Denmark and completed his schooling there. For higher studies, he enrolled in a university in the US, and completed both his bachelor's and master's degrees there. Since then, he has travelled to many other countries around the world. Ashar is now in Congo as a member of a voluntary organisation. His main job is to take care of children's education in a community school. His group has ten other members, all from different countries. Ashar is a nice fellow and has become a good friend of ours. We call him 'Mr Global Citizen'. I was talking to him the other day, and mentioned how impressed I am that he has been to so many countries. I asked him how he felt about that, and he said: "It's really nice to work with different people. I get to know so much about them — their language, family life, culture, their thoughts and aspirations. I sometimes think I belong to all." "Well, Ashar, you're a true global citizen," I said. "Aren't you too, Reza?" smiled Ashar Santoso. "We're all part of the same human race, aren't we?"

Stop, Look, and Listen
No author credited on this page
"Stop, Look, and Listen"
Is a very good rule to use
Not just before you cross a street,
But when you look for clues.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.

In this way, they will be able to support their families better, as well as contribute more effectively to the development of our economy.

André
Gwendolyn Brooks
I had a dream last night. I dreamed
I had to pick a mother out.
I had to choose a father too.
At first, I wondered what to do,
There were so many there, it seemed,
Short and tall and thin and stout.
But just before I sprang awake,
I knew what parents I would take.
And this surprised and made me glad:
They were the ones I always had!

Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.

It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.

What would you like to know? Sohan: Well, what's a good time to visit there? Dr. Arman: I think you can visit any time. The weather is more or less the same. Sohan: Good! And what should I see there? Dr. Arman: Well, you can visit the Cairo Museum and you should see the mummies. And you mustn't leave Cairo without visiting the Pyramids. Sohan: Anything else? Dr. Arman: Oh yes. Let's Play
Kate Greenaway
School is over,
Oh, what fun!
Lessons finished,
Play begun.
Who'll run fastest,
You or I?
Who'll laugh loudest?
Let us try.

Holding Hands
Leonore M Link
Elephants walking
Along the trails
Are holding hands
By holding tails.
Trunks and tails
Are handy things
When elephants walk
In Circus rings.
And when they walk—
It never fails
They're holding hands
By holding tails.
(Abridged)

Boats Sail on the Rivers
Christina Georgina Rossetti
Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;
But clouds that sail across the sky
Are prettier far than these.
There are bridges on the rivers,
As pretty as you please;
But the bow that bridges heaven,
And overtops the trees,
And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.

The Chaos
Gerard Nolst Trenité
I take it you already know
Of tough and bough and cough and dough?
Others may stumble, but not you
On hiccough, thorough, slough and through?
Beware of heard, a dreadful word
That looks like beard and sounds like bird.
And dead: it's said like bed, not bead --
For goodness' sake, don't call it 'deed'!
Watch out for meat and great and threat,
They rhyme with suite and straight and debt.
A moth is not the moth in mother,
Nor both in bother, broth, or brother.
And here is not a match for there,
Nor dear and fear for bear and pear.
And then there's dose and rose and lose -
Just look them up -- and goose and choose.
A dreadful language? Why, sakes alive!
I'd learned to speak it when I was five.
And yet, to write it, the more I tried,
I hadn't learned it at fifty-five.
(Abridged)

Every Wednesday, Class Six spends twenty minutes caring for a small garden behind the school library. Their teacher, Ms Rahman, helped them make a plan, but the pupils chose the plants. They planted spinach, beans and marigolds in three separate beds. A narrow path lets everyone walk between the beds without stepping on young plants.

At first, the children carried water in open buckets. Much of it spilled on the path. Rupa suggested using old bottles with small holes in their caps. The bottles helped the pupils water the roots slowly. The teacher checked that the bottles had no sharp edges before anyone used them.

The class keeps a notebook beside the library window. Each group records the weather, the plants' growth and the work it has done. When some leaves turned yellow, the pupils did not immediately add more water. They asked their teacher for help and compared their notes.

After the first harvest, the class shared the vegetables with the school kitchen. The children were proud, not because their garden was large, but because they had learned to work together and use resources carefully.
